overview: This entry is the Edo kingdom around Benin City in present-day Nigeria, not the modern Republic of Benin farther west. Its imported 1878 to 1914 interval spans both a living royal state and the British conquest of 1897. Court art and excavated homes and workshops illuminate the people within that transition.

periods.title: Late royal Benin
periods.summary: A court society with specialized craft traditions faced growing British imperial pressure.

periods.title: Conquest and colonial occupation
periods.summary: British forces captured and looted Benin City; the oba was exiled and colonial buildings replaced parts of the palace.

periods.title: Restoration with reduced powers
periods.summary: Eweka returned kingship to the rebuilt palace under colonial government; this was not restored independence.

sections.title: The palace and the people who made it

items.text: Benin’s court distinguished rank through architecture, clothing, jewellery and access to particular materials. The oba stood within a wider world of chiefs, attendants and specialist makers. Elaborate court art records those relationships, not just one ruler’s tastes.

A brass-and-iron royal head at the Met is dated broadly to the late eighteenth or nineteenth century. Its high beaded collar and elaborate crown show how later court artists made royal status visible through the form of a face and its ornaments.

A new oba commissioned a cast portrait of his deceased father for a palace altar. Such heads connected current government with royal ancestors, whose influence was understood to continue. The object had a ritual role, rather than serving as an ordinary portrait on a shelf.

The late palace was capable of change. Oba Ovonramwen introduced corrugated metal roofing and imported mirrors in his own quarters, while older horizontally grooved earthen walls remained important signs of elite architecture.

sections.title: What archaeology can tell us about daily life

items.text: Excavations at the MOWAA campus revealed habitation areas, wells and cisterns among the remains of precolonial Benin City. Water storage and access belong beside brass casting in the city’s history: people needed reliable supplies for ordinary work and life.

The 2022 to 2024 excavations recovered more than 120,000 fragments of locally made pottery. These ordinary broken vessels dominate the finds, even though royal bronzes have attracted far more international attention.

A likely nineteenth-century workshop contained pits with scorched edges, charcoal and lead slag. Crucible fragments and metal finds are being analysed to investigate how craft production actually worked.

Plant studies identified oil palm, pearl millet, cotton and foxtail millet. Researchers are combining these remains with animal bones and pottery residues to reconstruct diet and economy. The findings do not yet justify inventing a complete family menu.

One pit held over a hundred glass bottles, some with nineteenth-century trademarks, together with large snail shells and iron. Researchers suggest a shrine, but keep that interpretation tentative: a bottle’s final use need not be the purpose for which it was made.

sections.title: Conquest, memory and a written language

items.text: British forces attacked Benin in 1897, removed thousands of objects and exiled the oba. National Museums Scotland’s collection includes pieces bought from dealers soon afterward. Museum ownership histories are therefore part of the history of conquest, not a neutral afterthought.

In 1914 the exiled oba’s son became Oba Eweka and rebuilt a smaller palace. Hereditary makers resumed producing royal works. Political independence had ended, but Edo kingship and artistic practice had not disappeared.

A later written Edo sample is “Ekhere vb’ Itan Ẹdo”, the title known in English as “A Short History of Benin”. Jacob Egharevba’s autobiography records its 1933 publication. This is a printed twentieth-century language example, explicitly later than the mapped interval.

Egharevba’s parents were long-distance traders, and his schooling took him between the Benin and Yoruba regions. He drafted his history in 1921 and later studied by correspondence. His life shows how local historical knowledge and new forms of education could meet.

ending.text: The British conquest of 1897 ended the independent kingdom. Royal restoration in 1914 took place within colonial rule; Benin City and Edo communities continued, as did kingship and craft traditions.
